classification.difficultyReason: Compare straight-line extrapolations with the flattening data pattern and infer a nonlinear trend that avoids the line’s unrealistic zero-density prediction.

content.prompt: The plot shows the density of the rabbit population per square kilometre mapped against altitude in a region. Draw a line of best fit on the scatterplot.

spec.description: Writable scatterplot with eleven blue diamond markers, rectangular grid and no supplied best-fit line.
spec.answerVisibility: Data and grid are permanent student givens; the best-fit line belongs only in solutions.

children.label: a
children.prompt: An altitude of 0 m indicates sea level. What does your line of best fit imply will happen to the density of the rabbit population if the land were to dip below sea level?

answer.short: The line predicts that rabbit density would increase below sea level. This extrapolation may be unreliable.
answer.worked: Extending the negatively sloping line to altitudes below $0$ m gives higher rabbit densities. These altitudes are outside the observed range, so the relationship may change and the prediction may be unreliable.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Where does your line of best fit intersect the horizontal axis and what does this imply?

answer.short: For example, around $10\,000$ m, implying zero rabbits per square kilometre. The intercept depends on your line.
answer.worked: Extend the drawn line to rabbit density $0$ and read the altitude at its horizontal-axis intercept. An example line meets the axis at about $10\,000$ m, predicting zero rabbits per square kilometre there. Other reasonable by-eye lines give different intercepts. The plotted density near $10\,000$ m is still positive, showing a limitation of this linear model.

spec.description: Complete solution graph showing one acceptable by-eye example line through approximately (0,500) and (10000,0).
spec.mathematics: The example line has a horizontal-axis intercept of 10000 m; this is illustrative, not a unique regression answer.

children.label: c
children.prompt: By observing the flow of the data points, what can you suggest is the true trend at higher altitudes?

answer.short: Rabbit density appears to decrease nonlinearly, flattening towards a low positive density at higher altitudes.
answer.worked: The data fall steeply at first, then the decline becomes less steep. This suggests a nonlinear decreasing relationship: rabbit density remains low and may approach zero gradually, rather than reaching zero at the intercept of a straight line.
